Se ha notado que estas sílabas duran un poco más que las no acentuadas. El acento prosódico no se indica en el alfabeto. Como se ha explicado en la sección 2.5, el acento ortográfico en el mixteco indica el tono alto, mientras que en español indica el acento prosódico.
new_statements.translation: 2.6. Prosodic stress. All Mixtec words are stressed on the penultimate syllable (the syllable before the last syllable of the word). It has been noted that these syllables last a little longer than the unstressed ones. Prosodic stress is not indicated in the alphabet. As explained in section 2.5, the written accent in Mixtec indicates high tone, whereas in Spanish it indicates prosodic stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable of every word; its phonetic correlate is slightly greater duration. Stress is fully predictable and therefore unwritten; the acute accent of the orthography marks high tone, not stress. The language has three lexical tones (high, mid, low; sec. 2.5, p. 17), so this is a tone language with a fixed: penultimate syllable stress statement. Sec. 2.3 (p. 15) adds that the glottal stop (saltillo) occurs after a vowel of the penultimate syllable, 'the syllable that carries the prosodic stress'.
new_statements.exceptions: Only an intonational one: when vocatives are called from afar they are lengthened, 'la segunda sílaba recibe el acento prosódico y se alarga esa sílaba' and a final low tone is added (p. 32); the shift does not apply when the vocative is followed without pause by another word in the same sentence.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('todas las palabras'); statement made in the alphabet/orthography chapter of a popular grammar, not an instrumental study. Describes the Mixtec of San Andrés Yutatío, municipio de Tezoatlán, distrito de Huajuapan de León (Mixteca Baja), from the author's fieldwork since 1986.
new_statements.identity_note: The source describes the Mixtec of San Andrés Yutatío, municipio de Tezoatlán de Segura y Luna, Oaxaca (ISO mxb = Glottolog tezo1238; author's fieldwork since 1986). INALI treats the municipality as four variantes (es.wikipedia), with San Andrés Yutatío under 'mixteco del oeste alto'; the SIL page states the ten towns are mutually intelligible. The statement should be catalogued as Tezoatlán Mixtec (tezo1238), San Andrés Yutatío variety.

new_statements.quote: 2.6. Acento prosódico. Todas las palabras del mixteco se acentúan en la penúltima sílaba (la sílaba antes de la última sílaba de la palabra). Se ha notado que estas sílabas duran un poco más que las no acentuadas. El acento prosódico no se indica en el alfabeto. El saltillo se presenta después de cualquier vocal en la penúltima sílaba (la sílaba antes de la última sílaba). Esta sílaba tiene el acento prosódico (véase 2.6). [p. 15] ... Para llamar de lejos, la entonación causa los siguientes cambios: Se alargan los vocativos. La segunda sílaba recibe el acento prosódico y se alarga esa sílaba [p. 32]
new_statements.translation: 2.6. Prosodic stress. All Mixtec words are stressed on the penultimate syllable (the syllable before the last syllable of the word). It has been noted that these syllables last a little longer than the unstressed ones. Prosodic stress is not indicated in the alphabet. As explained in section 2.5, the written accent in Mixtec indicates high tone, whereas in Spanish it indicates prosodic stress. [p. 18] ... The saltillo (glottal stop) occurs after any vowel of the penultimate syllable (the syllable before the last syllable). This syllable carries the prosodic stress (see 2.6). [p. 15] ... To call from afar, intonation causes the following changes: vocatives are lengthened. The second syllable receives the prosodic stress and that syllable is lengthened [p. 32]

new_statements.relation_note: This is the very work the existing statement was taken from; the listed open_url (sil.org/mexico/mixteca/tezoatlan/G009a-GramMixTez-mxb.htm) is 404 live, but its the Internet Archive 2010-02-26 capture is the SIL-Mexico landing page linking 5.2 MB, 310 pp.), the same PDF already held by the project (310 PDF pp.). Re-reading confirms the catalog penultimate stress (penultimate) verbatim on p. 18 and adds the phonetic correlate (duration), the glottal-stop distribution and the vocative intonation exception.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Every word is stressed on the penultimate syllable; stressed syllables are somewhat longer; stress is fully regular and so unwritten (the written accent marks high tone instead). The glottal stop is confined to the stressed penult. Three lexical tones (high, mid, low) with extensive sandhi are independent of stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Vocatives called from a distance: the vocative is lengthened, the second syllable takes the stress and is lengthened, and a low tone is added (p. 32) - an intonational exception, not lexical. Nothing said about stress in words with attached dependent-pronoun suffixes (e.g. ndáa̱ + -í = ndáí 'mi mano', p. 18).
new_statements.identity_note: Work 1 describes the variety of San Andrés Yutatío, municipio de Tezoatlán, distrito de Huajuapan de León, Oaxaca (Mixteca Baja; author's fieldwork from 1986); the landing page and PDF metadata carry ISO code mxb. Work 0 describes the Silacayoapan dialect of Mixtec [mks], data collected May 1972-April 1973 in San Jerónimo Progreso, Municipio de Silacayoapan (note 1, p. 33), i.e. not tezo1238.

Sec. 2.3 (p. 15): the glottal stop occurs after a vowel of the penultimate syllable, 'esta sílaba tiene el acento prosódico'. Vocatives called from afar (p. 32) lengthen and shift stress to the second syllable (intonational). Three lexical tones (sec. 2.5, p. 17).
